prompt: Charge is quantised as q = ne, where n must be a {{1}} number.
explanation: A whole number. Charge comes in coins, not in liquid: you can have 3 electrons or 4, never three and a half. That is why the charge of any object is always an exact multiple of 1.602 x 10^-19 C.

prompt: Coulomb's law is an inverse square law, so tripling the distance between two charges drops the force to a ninth.
explanation: True. F = k q1 q2 over r squared, and three squared is nine. It is the standard sanity check on any force answer: doubling the distance quarters the force, halving it quadruples the force. The same square appears in the FIELD but not in the potential.

why.true: Correct. Three squared is nine, so the force falls to one ninth.
why.false: Wrong. The r is squared, so the effect of distance is much stronger than proportional.

prompt: The electric field E = F/q may be quoted in newtons per coulomb or, equivalently, in volts per {{1}}.
explanation: Volts per metre. The two units are the same thing seen from two definitions: E = F/q gives N/C, and E = V/d gives V/m. Test 1 uses Vm^-1 while Test 2 uses N/C, so both must be recognised on sight.

prompt: Step 1 of the method is to read the question twice and underline what is asked for.
explanation: True, and the reason is blunt: many marks are lost answering a question that was not set. Test 1 question 13 asks for the field produced by the NEGATIVE charge, and using the other one gives an answer that appears on the option list, so the error is invisible without careful reading.

why.true: Correct, and it is first because everything after it is wasted if the question was misread.
why.false: Wrong. It is step 1 precisely because the rest of the method depends on knowing what was asked.

prompt: Step 5 says to substitute the numbers first and then rearrange the formula.
explanation: The other way round. Rearrange in SYMBOLS first, and substitute numbers only at the end. Rearranging an expression that already contains numbers is where reciprocal and sign errors breed: get E = mg/q on the page before a single digit appears, and all that remains is arithmetic.

why.true: Wrong. That is the order that causes the errors the step exists to prevent.

prompt: Step 7 asks three things: is the size believable, is the {{1}} right, and does the sanity check apply?
explanation: The unit. Together with size and the sanity checks it catches most of what goes wrong: a capacitance of 4.77 farads is not believable, an answer in newtons where volts were wanted has the wrong unit, and a parallel resistance above its smallest member is impossible. Steps 3 and 7 save the most marks and are skipped the most often.

prompt: In a conductor charge moves freely, while in an insulator charge is {{1}} and cannot move freely.
explanation: Bound. Both materials are full of charge; the difference is whether it can travel. That single word explains why a conductor has no interior field, its free charges rearranging until everything cancels, and why an insulator instead polarises, its bound charges shifting slightly into dipoles without leaving home.

prompt: Why does the field formula take the MAGNITUDE of the charge, written E = k|Q|/r squared?

options.text: Because the formula returns the size of the field, while the sign is used separately to fix its direction
Because the field of a negative charge is zero
Because the bars mean the same as brackets
Because r squared is always positive

explanation: A field has a direction, not a negative size. Feeding a negative Q into the arithmetic would give a negative field strength, which means nothing. So the magnitude gives the number, and the sign is spent afterwards on the direction: away from a positive charge, towards a negative one.

why.a: Correct. Size from the magnitude, direction from the sign, in two separate steps.
why.b: Wrong. Charges are routinely negative, and Test 1 question 13 uses one.
why.c: Wrong. A negative charge has a perfectly ordinary field; it simply points inward.
why.d: Wrong. Bars mean absolute value, brackets merely group.
why.e: Wrong. That is true but has nothing to do with why the bars are on the Q.

prompt: Using the fan and vacuum picture, a positive charge is a fan blowing outward and a negative charge is a vacuum sucking inward. What happens midway between one of each?

options.text: Both send you the same way, so the two fields ADD
They push you in opposite directions, so the fields cancel
Neither has any effect at the midpoint
The fan wins because it is positive
The field points at right angles to the line joining them

explanation: The fan blows you away from itself, to the right, and the vacuum pulls you towards itself, also to the right. Same direction, so they add, which is why Test 1 question 8 comes to 2.16 x 10^7 rather than zero. Two FANS would fight and cancel. Opposite signs add, same signs cancel, and most people guess that backwards.

why.a: Correct, and it is why the answer doubles rather than vanishing.
why.b: Wrong. That is what two charges of the SAME sign would do.
why.c: Wrong. Both act at the midpoint; they simply act the same way.
why.d: Wrong. Equal magnitudes at equal distances give equal contributions.
why.e: Wrong. Both contributions lie along the line joining the charges.
